title: Teaching on Purpose #22: Confidence, Not Chronology
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: In this issue of his Teaching on Purpose series, Adam Kohlbeck writes up a conversation with Olly, a primary English and professional development lead, on the purpose of utilising memory. Kohlbeck contrasts the common rolling window of retrieval practice, where the newest six weeks of content go in and the oldest drop out, with Olly's approach of letting pupils' confidence and accuracy decide what stays on the daily starter. In Year 6 maths a cumulative arithmetic starter grows as new question types are taught, and a skill leaves it only when around 98% of pupils get it right 98% of the time. Taken-off skills are then retrieved in a weekly test that mimics test conditions, and pupils with lingering misconceptions get targeted intervention, with holiday homework and a broader check on return. The piece ends with PE as a contrast, where retrieval aims at automatic responses under pressure, showing that the same purpose needs very different techniques by subject.
points: Choose what to retrieve by how secure pupils are, not by how recently it was taught, so that some skills remain on the starter for far longer than six weeks.
A cumulative arithmetic starter that adds new question types as they are taught keeps procedures retrieved daily and interrupts the forgetting curve.
Olly removes a skill from the daily starter at roughly 98% of pupils correct 98% of the time, deliberately building space to forget as a desirable difficulty.
Weekly test-like checks, targeted intervention and holiday homework set different gaps between retrievals according to each pupil's security.
Subject matters: in PE the aim is automaticity under pressure, so retrieval is tacit and driven by the skills about to be used.
quotes: Retrieval practice is now a familiar feature of most classrooms. Arithmetic starters, quizzes and ‘do nows’ have become part of the furniture in many of our schools. But how do we decide what goes into them and, just as importantly, what comes out?

A common approach is a rolling window: six questions covering the last six weeks of teaching. Each week, the newest content goes on and the oldest content drops off. It is tidy and easy to plan, but it means that every skill gets roughly the same amount of retrieval, regardless of how well pupils actually know it. After six weeks, it disappears and we hope it is still there when pupils need it in the test.
Olly’s view is that the decision should be driven by confidence and accuracy rather than by where a skill sits in the teaching sequence. That small shift changes a lot.

If Olly can see that 98% of pupils are getting a question type right 98% of the time, that is when it comes off the daily starter. The few pupils who still hold a misconception are picked up in a separate intervention rather than holding the whole class back.
The core of the technique stays the same throughout: the gap between retrieval opportunities is set by the teacher’s judgement of how secure each pupil is, not by the calendar.

The key difference is the kind of memory we are trying to build. In a game, a pupil with a ball coming towards them and an opponent closing in has a split second to respond. There is no time to consciously select the right piece of knowledge. So the aim in PE is to automate the response.

Olly’s examples are also a reminder that we often treat pedagogy as generic when the subject itself is one of the most important parts of the context. That matters for all of us, but perhaps most of all for primary teachers, who are asked to be experts across so many different subjects.
